metadata.title: Civic education, school climate, and gender in Latin American countries: A path analysis using ICCS 2016 data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICCS 2016 student data from five Latin American countries (Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Peru) and applies the ICCS-recommended complex survey replicate-weight approach when estimating means and multilevel path coefficients. In the methods, the authors state that the SPSS complex data function was used to calculate means with appropriate replicate weights, and that the multilevel path analysis in Mplus7 also used the appropriate replicate weights as outlined in the ICCS User Guide. The analytic unit is students at level 1 with classrooms (one per school) at level 2, so the weighting supports correct variance estimation under the ICCS sampling design. The manuscript does not name a specific weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), so the exact weight field cannot be extracted, but the replicate-weight procedure is explicitly used.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this paper are ICCS composite Likert-scaled scales for civic education and citizenship types, which are treated as scaled scores rather than PV-based achievement outcomes; therefore plausible values handling is not applicable. For missing data, the authors state that Mplus7 used missing data estimation to preserve as many cases as possible, but they do not specify the exact missing-data algorithm (e.g., FIML vs. MI). Given the explicit use of Mplus7 missing-data estimation, the extraction maps this to multiple_imputation, but the precise mechanism is not fully documented in the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is restricted to ICCS 2016 Grade 8 students from five Latin American countries: Chile, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, and Peru. The study uses seven ICCS school-factor composite scales related to civic education (e.g., civic learning at school, willingness to participate, open classroom climate, student interaction, abuse, student-teacher relations, value of participation) and three citizenship-type composites (personally responsible, conventional, social movement related). For the multilevel path analysis, the authors first compute gender mean differences across the seven civic education measures and then select the five measures with the largest gender differences for subsequent modeling: abuse at school, perception of open classroom climate, civic learning at school, value of participation, and willingness to participate in school activities. The multilevel path models include gender, civic knowledge, and SES as controls, and Mplus7 missing-data estimation is used to preserve cases.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Grade 8 (Latin America subset) — civic education school factors predicting personally responsible citizenship
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel path coefficients (standardized betas) by country; e.g., Dominican Republic Model 1: Civic Learning 0.17*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.26* and Civic Learning*Gender interaction −0.17*; Mexico Model 1: Civic Learning 0.20*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.24* and Civic Learning*Gender −0.10*; Colombia Model 1: Civic Learning 0.17*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.23* and Civic Learning*Gender −0.07*; Chile Model 1: Civic Learning 0.19*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.24* and Civic Learning*Gender −0.09*; Peru Model 1: Civic Learning 0.24*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.25* and Civic Learning*Gender −0.04 (interaction not marked as significant in the table). Model fit: CFI ranges 0.905–0.984; RMSEA ranges 0.019–0.042; Standardized RMR within ranges 0.016–0.067.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Grade 8 data from Chile, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, and Peru, the study leveraged civic learning at school, school participation, participation in activities, open classroom climate, and abuse at school (with gender, SES, and civic knowledge controls) to predict personally responsible citizenship, finding positive main effects of civic learning and participation measures and statistically significant gender moderation via the civic learning × gender interaction in multiple countries (e.g., Dominican Republic, Chile, Colombia, Peru). This indicates that strengthening classroom civic learning and participation opportunities may support personally responsible citizenship differently for boys versus girls, so gender-responsive civic education design is needed, though the study is correlational and not causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Grade 8 (Latin America subset) — civic education school factors predicting conventional citizenship
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel path coefficients (standardized betas) by country; e.g., Dominican Republic Model 1: Civic Learning 0.13*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.18*; Mexico Model 1: Civic Learning 0.16*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.17*; Colombia Model 1: Civic Learning 0.20*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.26*; Chile Model 1: Civic Learning 0.21*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.24*; Peru Model 1: Civic Learning 0.19*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.24* with Civic Learning*Gender interaction −0.13* (significant). Model fit: CFI ranges 0.927–0.962; RMSEA ranges 0.034–0.042; Standardized RMR within ranges 0.027–0.067.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Grade 8 data from Chile, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, and Peru, the study leveraged civic learning at school, participation in activities, open classroom climate, and abuse at school (with gender, SES, and civic knowledge controls) to predict conventional citizenship, finding generally positive associations for civic education measures but a negative civic knowledge relationship with conventional citizenship across countries and a statistically significant gender moderation for civic learning in Peru (Civic Learning*Gender −0.13*). This indicates that conventional citizenship may be fostered through civic learning and participation, but gender-differentiated effects and the role of civic knowledge should be considered when designing civic curricula, while causality cannot be inferred from the cross-sectional path analysis.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Grade 8 (Latin America subset) — civic education school factors predicting social movement citizenship
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel path coefficients (standardized betas) by country; e.g., Dominican Republic Model 1: Civic Learning 0.16*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.21* and Civic Learning*Gender interaction −0.09*; Mexico Model 1: Civic Learning 0.17*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.19* and Civic Learning*Gender −0.03 (not marked significant); Colombia Model 1: Civic Learning 0.12*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.19* and Civic Learning*Gender −0.10*; Chile Model 1: Civic Learning 0.18*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.21* and Civic Learning*Gender −0.06 (not marked significant); Peru Model 1: Civic Learning 0.20*; Model 2: Civic Learning 0.21* and Civic Learning*Gender −0.01 (not marked significant). Model fit: CFI ranges 0.911–0.984; RMSEA ranges 0.019–0.042; Standardized RMR within ranges 0.016–0.067.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Grade 8 data from Chile, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, and Peru, the study leveraged civic learning at school, participation in activities, open classroom climate, and abuse at school (with gender, SES, and civic knowledge controls) to predict social movement citizenship, finding positive main effects of civic learning and participation measures and statistically significant gender moderation via civic learning × gender in the Dominican Republic and Colombia. This indicates that civic learning emphasizing participation and rights-related content may translate into social-movement citizenship more strongly for boys in some contexts, suggesting that civic education reforms should monitor and adjust for gender-differentiated engagement pathways.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses ICCS 2016 Grade 8 data from five Latin American countries (Chile, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, and Peru) to examine how school civic-education factors relate to three citizenship types and whether these relationships differ by gender. The authors first compute gender mean differences across seven civic education scales (standardized to mean 50, SD 10) and then select the five measures with the largest gender gaps for multilevel path analysis. The multilevel path models are estimated in Mplus7 using replicate weights and missing-data estimation to preserve cases, with students at level 1 and classrooms at level 2. Results are reported as standardized path coefficients and model fit indices (CFI, RMSEA, standardized RMR); for example, civic learning shows positive associations with all citizenship types, while civic knowledge has mixed/negative associations for conventional citizenship. The study is correlational (path analysis) and does not use ML algorithms, so findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.
